chunks: As for what he mentioned regarding covering the head: al-Shaykh, may Allah the Exalted support him, informed me from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, from his father, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Abi Abdillah, from Ali ibn Asbat, or a man from him, from the one who narrated it, from Abi Abdillah عليه السلام:
That he used to do this: when he entered the privy, he would cover his head and say quietly to himself: “In the Name of Allah, and by Allah.”

Then he mentioned and said: when he reaches the place in which he relieves himself, he should put forward his left foot before the right, and say: “In the Name of Allah, and by Allah. I seek refuge in Allah from the filthy, impure, wicked, corrupting accursed Shaytan.” Then he should sit and not face [forward].

(1) For that is recommended in order to distinguish between it and entering the masjid, because when the masjid is among the noble places, it is recommended that one first place into it the noble limb, which is the right foot; and the place of relief is the opposite of that, so entering it with the left foot was chosen. Then he said: and say—and he mentioned the supplication. (2)

key_terms.الرِّجْسِ النِّجْسِ: filth and impurity from which refuge is sought
key_terms.الْخَلَاءُ: the place of relief or toilet area
key_terms.الْكَنِيفَ: the privy or place of relieving oneself
key_terms.الْمَسْجِدِ: the masjid, contrasted here with the place of relief in matters of etiquette
key_terms.بِسْمِ اللَّهِ وَبِاللَّهِ: a brief invocation said upon entering, meaning in Allah’s Name and by Allah
key_terms.تَغْطِيَةِ الرَّأْسِ: covering the head as an act of recommended etiquette

ai.seo_question: What are the recommended etiquettes and supplications when entering the toilet in Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith reports the etiquette of entering the place of relief: covering the head, quietly saying “Bismillah wa billah,” entering with the left foot, and seeking refuge in Allah from the accursed Shaytan. It also notes the juristic reasoning for preferring the left foot here in contrast to entering the masjid with the right foot, highlighting distinctions in ritual etiquette and taharah.
